content.thinking:
I need to be careful here—the error rate itself didn't spike, but memory usage climbing toward its limit is the real harm signal. I should distinguish what's actually documented in the record versus what the candidate claims about latency, since only the heap log data is confirmed in the record.

So the causal chain: memory rose steadily while errors stayed flat, pointing to heap growth toward the limit with no corresponding traffic change. The leak itself was never pinpointed to specific code—only that a restart resolved it, so the root cause of which allocation is leaking remains unconfirmed, with a fix only proposed afterward.

For contributing factors, I'm noting the alert fired well after heap warnings began, and the alert's description didn't match what it detects—both gaps worth flagging as action items, alongside the need for earlier trend-based alerting and a longer-term fix since the restart was only a temporary patch. I'll keep the numbers vague, avoiding specific figures or memory limits, and keep the action items to a short, focused list of three.

For lessons learned, what went well was the quick restart and confirmation; what went wrong was the late alert and the mismatched label. We got lucky that heap usage stayed under the limit before the restart happened and that there wasn't a traffic spike complicating things. I should also flag that the leak's root cause is still assumed rather than confirmed, and the investigator's latency claims weren't substantiated in the record, so I won't include them.

action_items.item: Add an early-warning alert on sustained heap growth, or heap usage approaching the limit, on io-shop. It should fire well before memory is close to exhaustion.
Fix the HighMemoryUsage alert so its description matches the series its rule evaluates (memory, not error rate).
Add a soak or memory-growth check, run before release or in staging, that fails when heap keeps growing under steady load.

causal_chain.step: Memory use on io-shop rose from {series_before} to an average of {series_while_broken} and a peak of {series_at_worst}, putting the service at risk of running out of memory. The error rate did not rise: {errors_before} before, {errors_while_broken} during. The logs show the heap warnings and the usual background error noise, but no new failures.
The heap grew steadily toward the memory limit. The warnings came every minute from about 15:45 and peaked at the last reading before the restart.

Nothing external explains the growth. No production changes were recorded in either lookback window, and no flag changes were recorded. The metrics show request volume flat, so this was not load outgrowing capacity.

The most likely explanation is that the process never released some memory, such as a heap object or a pool. A restart returned the service to baseline, and the paging rule stopped firing. That supports a leak inside the process, but the record does not show which code leaks.

contributing_factors.factor: The restart only clears the symptom. Until the leak is fixed, memory will climb again after every restart.

Detection was late. The climb started at {began}, and heap warnings appeared roughly a quarter of an hour before the page at {alert_raised}. Nothing warned about a steady upward trend or approaching the limit.
The alert is named HighMemoryUsage but its text said error rate above threshold, while the error rate never rose. The mismatch makes it harder to see what the alert is measuring.
Nothing in testing or review catches a slow memory leak before it reaches production.

input.executive_summary: For about {duration}, from {began} until {recovered}, the shop service's memory use climbed steadily toward its limit. The share of failed requests did not rise: it was {errors_before} before and {errors_while_broken} during. Shoppers were not failing more often, but the service was heading toward running out of memory, which would have taken it down. The alert fired late, at {alert_raised}, well after the climb began. Argus restarted the service, which cleared the memory growth, and the paging rule stopped firing. Argus then drafted a fix as a pull request. It is not yet reviewed, so the underlying leak can return until it is merged.

got_lucky: The heap stayed below its limit until the restart, so the process was not killed for running out of memory and shoppers saw no extra failures.
Traffic stayed flat. A traffic rise would have brought the limit forward.
went_well: Argus picked up the alert within seconds, read metrics, logs and change history, and restarted the service within about a minute of the page.
The restart was checked against the paging rule and confirmed, and Argus drafted a fix pull request straight away.
went_wrong: The alert fired late, after the memory climb had been under way for a long time.
The alert's name and text disagreed, and the series it watches rose without any rise in failed requests.
The restart does not fix the leak, and the root allocation is still unidentified.

input.root_cause: The io-shop process kept memory it should have released, so its heap grew steadily toward its memory limit with no deploy, flag change or traffic increase to explain it. The record does not identify which allocation leaked; a restart cleared the growth, and the proposed fix is still unmerged.
input.symptom: Service memory climbed toward its limit
